common_name: Giant Miscanthus (Biomass Grass, Elephant Grass Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this sterile hybrid produces no viable seed and must be propagated vegetatively, so start from nursery-grown rhizomes or divisions rather than seed.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving this giant grass plenty of room since a mature clump can tower 8-13 feet tall on stout, cane-like stems. A naturally occurring sterile triploid hybrid between Miscanthus sinensis and Miscanthus sacchariflorus, it forms dense, non-spreading clumps and cannot escape into the wild by seed the way some Miscanthus species can, making it a safer choice for large-scale plantings. Coarse, arching green leaves rise on tall canes through summer, and silvery-tan plumes appear in fall in warmer zones, though the display is grown chiefly for screening, biomass, and dramatic vertical structure rather than bloom. It takes two to three seasons to reach full size and mature root depth, after which it needs little input beyond an annual cutback. Cut the entire clump to the ground in late winter before new shoots emerge, since old canes do not regreen.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun (afternoon shade in hot climates); Dixieland is a compact sport of 'Variegatus' found as a seedling and stays noticeably smaller and more upright than its parent.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil that ranges from loose sand to heavy clay in full sun, giving afternoon shade in hot southern gardens; Dixieland is a dwarf, densely tufted form of the classic white-striped 'Variegatus' maiden grass, carrying the same bold, creamy-white longitudinal stripes on each blade but on a plant scaled to about half the size. Its more erect, compact habit resists the late-season flopping that can affect the taller 'Variegatus', so it rarely needs staking. Lavender-pink plumes emerge above the foliage in late summer and age to tan, adding a soft contrast to the crisp white-striped leaves. The strong variegation reads well from a distance, making it useful as a bright accent in front of dark evergreens or in large containers. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Kleine Fontane Maiden Grass (Compact Fountain-Form Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Kleine Fontane (Little Fountain) is a compact, RHS Award of Garden Merit-winning maiden grass suited to smaller gardens than full-size cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun; Kleine Fontane forms a dense, upright clump of narrow, arching green leaves marked with a fine white midrib. In mid to late summer it sends up airy, whisk-like plumes that emerge deep red before aging to shimmering silvery-white through fall, held gracefully above the foliage in a fountain-like spray that gives the cultivar its name. Fall color turns the foliage clear gold before it fades to tan for winter interest. Its moderate, well-behaved size makes it a good choice for mixed borders and smaller residential landscapes where larger miscanthus cultivars would overwhelm the space. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Sarabande has some of the narrowest, finest-textured leaves of any miscanthus cultivar and holds a strictly upright habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Sarabande is prized among maiden grass cultivars for its exceptionally fine, threadlike leaf blades striped with a crisp white midrib, giving the whole clump a soft, airy, fountain-like texture that catches light and moves easily in the slightest breeze. The habit stays strongly upright rather than arching or flopping, making it a reliable choice for a narrow accent or vertical screen without staking. Feathery, pink-to-red-tinged plumes rise well above the foliage from late summer into fall before fading to silvery tan, and the fine leaves turn gold before browning for winter interest. Its refined texture contrasts nicely with broad-leaved perennials and coarser grasses in a mixed border. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Undine is a mid-sized upright miscanthus cultivar grown for its dark green, white-midribbed foliage and purple-flushed late-summer plumes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun; Undine forms an upright, clump-forming mound of long, narrow, dark green leaves marked with a prominent white midvein that gives the foliage a cool, silvery cast from a distance. In late summer into early autumn, large plumes of purple-flushed, silver-white flowers rise above the foliage, aging to a soft tan and providing texture and movement through winter if left uncut. Foliage turns orange to straw-gold in fall before browning, extending the season of interest well past bloom. Its moderate height and sturdy, upright habit suit it to mixed borders, large containers, or as a seasonal screen without the need for staking. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches above ground in late winter before new shoots emerge.

common_name: Huron Sunrise Maiden Grass (Early-Blooming Burgundy-Plumed Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Huron Sunrise, selected in Ontario, blooms earlier than many miscanthus cultivars and is valued for its large, profuse burgundy plumes.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil from sandy to clay-based in full sun, where Huron Sunrise forms a graceful, upright, arching clump of green leaves marked with a silvery midrib. Bred in Ontario, Canada, it is valued for an unusually early and heavy bloom, sending up large, showy burgundy plumes in late summer well ahead of many later-flowering miscanthus cultivars, an important advantage for gardeners in cooler climates where a late-season bloomer may not flower before frost. The plumes fade to a soft creamy tan as they persist into fall and winter, while the foliage turns golden. Its excellent cold hardiness and reliable bloom timing make it one of the better maiden grass choices for northern gardens. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Totem Pole Switchgrass (Prairie Winds Narrow Columnar Steel-Blue Switchgrass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained to moist soil, from sand to clay, in full sun; Totem Pole is a Prairie Winds series switchgrass bred for an exceptionally narrow, strictly columnar form.

directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil from sand to clay in full sun; Totem Pole is a native switchgrass selection bred for a remarkably narrow, strictly upright column of steel-blue foliage on powdery blue stems, reaching about 6 feet tall while spreading only about 2.5 feet wide. That slim, non-flopping footprint makes it useful for adding vertical drama in beds too narrow for wide-spreading switchgrass cultivars, or as a repeated accent along a border. Golden seed panicles appear atop the clump in early fall, adding late-season texture and movement before fading to tan for winter interest. Like other switchgrass selections it carries the deep, fibrous root system of the wild prairie species, tolerates periodic flooding as well as drought once established, and is generally deer and rabbit resistant. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Apache Rose Switchgrass (Prairie Winds Pink-Plumed Blue-Green Switchgrass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Apache Rose, a Prairie Winds series switchgrass, is grown for its abundant pale pink plumes and blue-green foliage that flushes pink in fall.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Apache Rose forms an upright, columnar clump of blue-green foliage that shifts to warm pink tones as autumn approaches, complementing the abundant, airy, pale pink plumes it produces from late summer and holds well into winter. At roughly 4 feet tall and 2.5 feet wide it stays more compact than many switchgrass selections, fitting easily into perennial borders and smaller prairie-style plantings without staking. As a native switchgrass cultivar, it retains the deep root system and excellent drought tolerance of the wild species once established, tolerates a wide range of soils, and is generally resistant to deer and rabbit browsing. Cut the clump back to a few inches above the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Niagara Falls Switchgrass (Prairie Winds Wide-Arching Powder-Blue Switchgrass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in any well-drained to moist soil, from sand to clay, in full sun; Niagara Falls, a Prairie Winds series switchgrass, has notably wide, arching, powder-blue foliage reminiscent of miscanthus.

directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil from sand to clay in full sun; Niagara Falls stands out among switchgrass cultivars for its notably wide, gracefully arching, powder-blue foliage that gives it a fuller, more miscanthus-like presence in the landscape than the typically narrow, upright switchgrass form. At about 4 feet tall and equally wide, it fills space quickly and effectively, making it useful as a substantial specimen or informal low screen. Sprays of cream-colored seed heads pack the top of the clump in fall, and the sturdy foliage and stems generally remain standing through winter, providing valuable cover for birds. As a native switchgrass selection it is highly adaptable to soil type, tolerates both drought and periodic flooding once established, and needs no staking. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Blue Spear Switchgrass (Prairie Winds Steely Blue-Green Upright Switchgrass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Spear, a Prairie Winds series switchgrass, forms a strongly upright clump of steely blue-green foliage.

directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun, where Blue Spear's strong vertical form and cool, steely blue-green foliage are at their best; the upright, narrow silhouette makes it a clean accent for perennial borders and prairie-style plantings that need height and structure without a wide spread. Airy flower panicles rise above the foliage through summer and continue adding soft texture and movement into fall and winter. As a native switchgrass selection it is highly heat, humidity, and drought tolerant once established, generally deer and rabbit resistant, and needs no staking even in exposed sites. Cut the clump back to a few inches above the ground in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Burgundy Bunny Fountain Grass (Compact Red-Tipped Dwarf Fountain Grass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Burgundy Bunny is a very compact fountain grass selection whose foliage reddens through summer into deep red by fall.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun; Burgundy Bunny forms a tight, mounding tuft of fine-textured foliage that emerges green with burgundy-red tips in summer and deepens to solid red by fall, giving strong season-long color in a very small footprint. In mid to late summer, showy silvery-white flower spikes resembling miniature foxtails arch outward above the foliage. At only about 12-15 inches tall and wide, it is one of the smallest fountain grass selections available, well suited to container culture, border edging, and small-space plantings where full-size fountain grass would be too large. It is drought tolerant once established and essentially free of serious pests or disease. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Weserbergland Fountain Grass (Dwarf Bright-Green Fountain Grass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Weserbergland is a fast-growing dwarf fountain grass selection with bright green foliage and long-lasting white bottlebrush plumes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun; Weserbergland grows quickly into a dense, graceful, fountain-shaped clump of bright green, fine-textured foliage that turns golden brown in autumn. From summer into fall it produces abundant white, bottle-brush-like flower spikes about 5-7 inches long that stand out well against the foliage before shattering in early winter. Its moderate, well-behaved size and high drought tolerance make it a reliable choice for mass plantings, mixed borders, and containers. It is largely free of serious pests and diseases once established. Cut the clump back to a few inches above ground in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Eaton Canyon Fountain Grass (Dwarf Purple-Bronze Fountain Grass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions after all danger of frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Eaton Canyon is a sterile dwarf purple fountain grass that will not reseed, unlike species-type purple fountain grass.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Eaton Canyon is a compact selection of purple fountain grass, staying a manageable 24-30 inches tall while spreading 3-5 feet, noticeably smaller than standard purple fountain grass. Finely textured, burgundy-bronze foliage forms a full, clumping mound, and feathery, pinkish, foxtail-like plumes rise above the leaves from late summer through fall, aging to a soft creamy buff. As a sterile selection it produces no viable seed, so it will not self-sow and become weedy the way species-type purple fountain grass can in warm climates. It is heat and drought tolerant once established and generally resistant to deer. In zones below its hardiness range, grow it as a container annual or overwinter divisions indoors. Cut back hard in late winter or early spring where it survives as a perennial.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; pine muhly is native to the southwestern United States and Mexico and forms a tidy, fountain-shaped clump of fine, needle-like foliage that reads almost evergreen.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; pine muhly forms a dense, tidy, fountain-shaped clump of stiff, finely textured, needle-like green foliage that gives it an almost pine-like, semi-evergreen look distinct from most other muhly grasses. From late summer through fall, thin flower stalks rise above the foliage bearing mauve-tinted plumes that age to a creamy tan, adding a soft haze of color and texture without overwhelming the clump. Native to rocky slopes and canyons of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, it thrives in well-drained, often rocky soil and is exceptionally drought tolerant once established, needing little supplemental water. Its fine texture and year-round structure make it a good choice for xeriscape plantings, rock gardens, and as a textural contrast to broader-leaved desert perennials. Trim back old foliage in late winter to keep the clump tidy before new growth resumes.

common_name: El Toro Bull Grass (Compact Rosy-Purple-Plumed Muhly Selection)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, rocky to average soil in full sun to partial shade; El Toro is a compact selection of bullgrass chosen for its showy rosy-purple flower spikes, originally collected in southeastern Arizona.

directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky to average soil in full sun, where it also tolerates reflected heat from paving and walls; El Toro forms a compact, dense clump of long, blue-green leaves with a slightly coarse texture, staying noticeably smaller than the straight species bullgrass. In fall it sends up masses of loose, showy, rosy-purple flower spikes that dry to tan through winter, the trait for which this selection was originally chosen from a wild population in southeastern Arizona. It tolerates a wide range of soils and handles both full sun and light shade, though flowering is best in full sun. A vigorous cutback in early spring, removing dormant foliage and spent flower spikes, keeps the clump tidy and encourages fresh new growth. Once established it is highly drought tolerant and needs no supplemental irrigation.
